# Hood Unlatches but Won't Pop Up: A Mechanical Failure Pattern

This specific failure mode on a 1998 Volvo V70 presents a distinct mechanical paradox that differs significantly from standard latch seizure issues. The symptom you described—where the primary release lever disengages the main catch, yet the hood remains grounded until manual lift breaks the secondary safety lock—is indicative of an alignment or linkage geometry problem rather than simple corrosion. When two people are required to operate it, one person is effectively providing the leverage needed to clear the safety latch before the hood can fully rotate open.

In most automotive designs, the primary release cable pulls a lever that rotates a catch arm away from the locking stud. Once this occurs, gravity and the weight of the lifted hood should allow the secondary safety pin or hook to slide out of its track. If your hood unlatches but refuses to rise an inch or two, the safety latch is likely not sliding along its intended path because it is physically obstructed by a misaligned cable end or a bent catch arm. When you release the handle and the latches snap back shut immediately, it confirms that the tension required to hold the secondary pin open was never established in the first place.

Your attempt to lubricate the assembly with WD-40 addressed surface friction but failed to resolve the underlying kinematic issue. While penetrating oil is excellent for removing rust from stationary parts, it cannot force a bent metal component back into alignment or adjust a cable that has stretched over 25 years of use. The fact that the release handle moved "a bit smoother" suggests the internal mechanism was sticky, but the lack of upward motion indicates the linkage geometry is still off.

To diagnose this without fully disassembling the hood, you should inspect the cable routing from the interior lever to the engine bay latch assembly. Over time, the plastic guide tubes or the cable itself can fray, causing the end of the cable to slide deeper into the barrel than designed. If the cable is too long effectively, it pulls the catch arm partway out but not enough to clear the safety track. Conversely, if the cable has stretched significantly, the lever may feel like it's doing work, but the force never reaches the threshold needed to fully retract the primary latch arm away from the safety hook.

The most effective repair involves removing the hood support strut and accessing the latch assembly from underneath or by tilting the hood slightly while supported. Once exposed, you must manually manipulate the catch arms to ensure they are not bent. You may need to trim a few millimeters off the end of the release cable if it is protruding too far, ensuring that when the lever is pulled, the arm rotates fully clear of the safety track before the hood attempts to lift.

Another possibility specific to this era of Volvo is a broken spring within the latch mechanism itself. These springs are responsible for snapping the hood shut and holding the safety pin in place until released. If the tension spring has fatigued or snapped, the safety pin might not slide out smoothly when the primary latch opens. In such cases, replacing the entire latch assembly is often more cost-effective than attempting to repair individual components, as these units are rarely sold separately from the housing.

If you decide to proceed with adjustment, be cautious about over-tightening any fasteners securing the latch to the chassis. Forcing a misaligned latch back into place can strip threads in the stamped steel chassis holes, turning a simple alignment fix into a structural repair requiring welding or patch plates. Always test the operation incrementally after each adjustment to ensure the safety lock engages correctly when the hood is lowered but allows full lift when commanded.

The key takeaway is that smoothness of operation does not guarantee correct geometric alignment; the hood must travel its full range without binding at the secondary safety point to be considered functional.
